title: Ribociclib + endocrine therapy · metastatic

agents.name: Ribociclib
agents.explanation: Ribociclib blocks CDK4 and CDK6, proteins that help cells move through the cycle of division. Endocrine therapy reduces the hormone signal that can drive HR-positive breast cancer.
agents.watch: Keep blood and ECG appointments. Fever, jaundice, fainting, palpitations, severe rash or new breathlessness need prompt advice.
risks: Rare serious lung or skin reactions

agents.name: AI or fulvestrant
agents.explanation: An aromatase inhibitor (AI) lowers oestrogen production; fulvestrant blocks and reduces oestrogen receptors. These are alternative endocrine partners, selected by the team. Ovarian suppression is needed in pre/perimenopausal patients.
agents.watch: The endocrine medicine continues during the ribociclib week off. Report troublesome joint, menopausal or injection-site symptoms.
risks: Hot flushes, joint pain and fatigue
Bone loss with AI / ovarian suppression

purpose: Ribociclib with an aromatase inhibitor or fulvestrant aims to control advanced HR-positive/HER2-negative breast cancer. The exact endocrine partner depends on previous treatment and menopausal status.
schedule_summary: The usual metastatic starting dose is ribociclib 600 mg once daily on Days 1–21 followed by Days 22–28 off. Continue the prescribed AI daily or fulvestrant on its own injection schedule; add ovarian suppression when indicated. Continue while beneficial and tolerated.

phases_note: A general pathway, not an appointment calendar. Your team confirms the order, overlap and duration; no date entry is needed.
timeline_note: Treatment bands show the source schedule. Symptom bands show possible patterns, not measured probabilities; serious effects can occur at any time.
safety_note: Fever, shivers or suddenly feeling unwell require immediate contact. Serious symptoms override the timeline or diary.
teachback: Which medicine is taken when, which test is due next, who reviews it, and which symptoms mean you should call today?
consent_support: Discuss the treatment aim, alternatives, benefit and uncertainty, important medicine-specific risks, reproductive precautions, symptom support and planned duration. Confirm the endocrine partner and any ovarian-suppression plan. The timeline does not authorise a restart or certify clinical review.
urgent_extra: Report new breathlessness, chest symptoms, severe diarrhoea, inability to drink, jaundice, a painful swollen leg or a severe rash promptly. You do not need to identify which medicine caused the symptom.

support.title: Nausea support
support.text: NCCP classifies ribociclib as oral moderate–high emetic risk. The team chooses preventive or rescue antiemetics using local policy, symptoms, QT risk and drug interactions; do not reuse another regimen’s prescription.

support.title: Electrolytes and heart rhythm
support.text: Correct abnormal potassium, calcium, magnesium and phosphate as directed. Attend the baseline and cycle 1 Day-14 ECG; fainting or palpitations need urgent advice.

support.title: Counts and liver tests
support.text: Keep the early two-weekly blood tests and subsequent monitoring. Report fever, shivers, jaundice or dark urine promptly.

support.title: Endocrine treatment
support.text: The AI or fulvestrant, and ovarian suppression when prescribed, continue on their own timetable. Discuss joint, menopausal, bone and injection-site symptoms.

support.title: Daily administration
support.text: Avoid grapefruit and check interactions. Do not replace a missed or vomited dose. A clinical hold requires explicit instructions about which medicine stops and who authorises restart.

questions.a: The usual metastatic starting dose is ribociclib 600 mg once daily on Days 1–21 followed by Days 22–28 off. Continue the prescribed AI daily or fulvestrant on its own injection schedule; add ovarian suppression when indicated. Continue while beneficial and tolerated. There is no fixed three-year stop in this metastatic regimen; the team reviews response, side effects and the next treatment decision.

questions.q: Which checks happen before and during treatment?
questions.a: FBC, renal and liver profile, potassium, calcium, magnesium and phosphorus. ECG before initiation; QTcF must be below 450 ms. Correct electrolyte abnormalities and review QT/CYP3A interactions. Confirm endocrine partner, menopause/ovarian suppression, prior treatment and the NCCP indication/eligibility discrepancy. FBC, renal and liver profile every two weeks for cycles 1–2, then before cycles 3–6, then as clinically indicated. Electrolytes before each of the first six cycles, then as clinically indicated; correct abnormalities. Repeat ECG around Day 14 of cycle 1, then as clinically indicated. Increase liver monitoring for grade 2 or worse abnormalities. Review fever, jaundice, palpitations/fainting, pulmonary and severe skin symptoms; response imaging follows the advanced-disease plan.

questions.q: Do I need to enter dates?
questions.a: No. This map shows general timing without personal information. Your hospital arranges actual appointments; ask who books each test and who reviews its result.

questions.q: What if a dose is missed or treatment is held?
questions.a: Take ribociclib once daily with or without food; swallow whole. Avoid grapefruit. If a dose is missed or vomited, do not take an extra dose; take the next scheduled dose. Confirm any clinical hold and restart with the team. The endocrine partner follows a separate prescription. A hold may affect one medicine rather than the whole combination; confirm each component.

questions.q: What does the evidence mean for me?
questions.a: Studies of ribociclib with hormone therapy in defined advanced-breast-cancer groups showed a survival benefit. The studies used different hormone partners and included different menopausal and prior-treatment groups. Ask which study matches your plan; the results do not set an individual time limit.

questions.q: What happens after treatment changes or ends?
questions.a: There is no fixed three-year stop in this metastatic regimen; the team reviews response, side effects and the next treatment decision. Keep the separately agreed disease follow-up, endocrine and bone-health plan.

evidence.title: MONALEESA-2, MONALEESA-3 and MONALEESA-7: separate populations and partners
evidence.intro: Studies describe groups. Ask how closely the treatment and study population match your situation.
evidence.population: MONALEESA-2: 668 postmenopausal women, first-line advanced disease. MONALEESA-3: 726 patients in first-/second-line fulvestrant contexts. MONALEESA-7: 672 pre/perimenopausal women with goserelin plus endocrine therapy. All had HR-positive/HER2-negative advanced disease.
evidence.interpretation: Studies of ribociclib with hormone therapy in defined advanced-breast-cancer groups showed a survival benefit. The studies used different hormone partners and included different menopausal and prior-treatment groups. Ask which study matches your plan; the results do not set an individual time limit.
evidence.limitations: Your team can discuss the strength and limitations of the evidence alongside treatment risks and alternatives.

sections.title: Before starting
sections.text: Confirm the exact medicine, strength, endocrine partner, baseline tests and first review appointments. Ask who arranges tests and who reviews the results.

sections.title: Taking treatment
sections.text: Take ribociclib once daily with or without food; swallow whole. Avoid grapefruit. If a dose is missed or vomited, do not take an extra dose; take the next scheduled dose. Confirm any clinical hold and restart with the team. The endocrine partner follows a separate prescription.

sections.title: Your endocrine partner has a separate timetable
sections.text: An aromatase inhibitor is normally taken daily through the targeted-medicine rest week. If fulvestrant is the chosen partner, the usual schedule is 500 mg by intramuscular injection on Days 1, 15 and 29, then once monthly; confirm the prescribed dose and appointment dates. Any ovarian-suppression injections have their own schedule.

sections.title: Treatment duration
sections.text: There is no fixed three-year stop in this metastatic regimen; the team reviews response, side effects and the next treatment decision.

sections.title: Supply and appointments
sections.text: Request the next supply before tablets run out. Blood tests and any ECG or injections need their own appointments. This oral treatment does not itself require a central line or infusion pump.

sections.title: If treatment is held
sections.text: Ask which medicine is held, whether the endocrine partner continues, what needs to recover, when the next review is due and who will authorise restart.

sections.title: Support between appointments
sections.text: Keep the oncology contact details and prescribed symptom medicines accessible. New severe symptoms need prompt assessment rather than waiting for the next blood test.

anatomy: Baseline ECG and an ECG around Cycle 1 Day 14. Fainting or palpitations need urgent advice.
Keep liver blood tests. Yellow skin / eyes, dark urine or marked upper-abdominal discomfort: call promptly.
Blood counts guide whether the next cycle can start. Fever, shivers or sudden illness: contact oncology immediately.
New cough or breathlessness needs prompt assessment, even between visits.
A widespread painful rash, blisters or peeling skin needs urgent assessment.
Discuss joint symptoms and keep the agreed bone-risk and DXA plan.
